title: Chapter XXXII

teacherSummary.text: Darcy calls on Elizabeth alone and is uneasy. Charlotte suspects he is in love; Elizabeth dismisses the idea. Darcy keeps meeting her on walks.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXXII,” how does Austen show puzzling visits? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXXII develops the idea of puzzling visits. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses irony in Chapter XXXII to complicate the reader's understanding of puzzling visits. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of puzzling visits responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXXII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of puzzling visits. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: What clues does Elizabeth miss? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include emergence, concise, counterbalance, patronage, journeys. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “It was absolutely necessary, therefore, to think of something, and in this emergence recollecting when she had seen him last in Hertfordshire, and feeling curious to know what he would say on the subject of their hasty departure, she observed—” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: The act of rising out of a fluid, or coming forth from envelopment or concealment, or of rising into view.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Unchaperoned meetings were noticeable in a small community. Now, why does this chapter matter? Dramatic irony: readers see what Elizabeth refuses to see. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Irony, Characterization, Foreshadowing.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot irony, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
